newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dlr can rise and not hurt exports - Thiessen.
newsitem.headline: Canada dlr can rise and not hurt exports - Thiessen.

text.p: Bank of Canada governor Gordon Thiessen on Wednesday said the Canadian dollar could rise at least another 1.5 percent without hurting Canada's export competitiveness.
"At the very least the currency can increase at the rate of 1.5 percent a year without affecting the competitiveness of our exports," Thiessen told reporters after a speech to college students.
Thiessen explained that that was possible because of the 1.5 percentage point inflation gap between Canada and the United States, Canada's main trade partner.
Thiessen was responding to reporters' queries as to whether the rallying Canadian dollar would affect Canada's exporting ability and prompt a reduction of Canadian interest rates in the near future.
Thiessen would not say whether it would be possible to ease monetary policy in the coming months in response to any further strengthening of the Canadian currency.
"That is going to depend on the strength of the economy. It's going to depend on what happens to interest rates outside our economy," Thiessen said.
But he noted that the 25 basis point drop in Canada's bank rate on October 2 was in fact a rebalancing of Canadian monetary monetary conditions in the face of a stronger domestic currency.
"Yes indeed, the last time around was a rebalancing of monetary conditions," Thiessen said.

Turning to the possibility the U.S. Federal Reserve may raise interest rates at the November 13 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, Thiessen said that if such an increase were to keep the United States on a non-inflationary economic growth path, "that would be good news for Canada".
"The best thing that can happen to us is for the U.S. economy to stay on a non-inflationary path because if it does, you're unlikely to have a serious recession in the U.S.," he said.
Thiessen said the comments by Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin earlier in the day that Canada was on track to lower budget deficits and eventually, a balanced budget, were encouraging.
"Everybody needs to be encouraged by the ongoing reduction that's being planned in the defict and eventually in the debt-to-GDP ratio," Thiessen said.

In his speech, which was delivered in French to a gathering of economics students and professors, Thiessen said the Bank of Canada's low-inflation monetary policy was fostering a climate conducive to sustained economic growth.
"At present, the Canadian economy is on the right track. It has made most of the necessary adjustments, and the conditions are right for strong expansion of demand," Thiessen said.
He said the central bank's current objective to maintain inflation within a range of one to three percent would not be re-evaluated until 1998.
After his speech Thiessen said the underlying fundamentals of the Canadian economy looked better than they had in the past 20 years.
